nameStory: The tuberous pea gets its name from the small, potato-like tubers that grow along its underground root system. These starchy tubers were once harvested and eaten in parts of Europe, earning it the alternate name "earthnut pea" - essentially meaning "underground nut pea." The scientific name Lathyrus tuberosus literally translates to "tuberous sweet pea," referencing both its edible roots and its relationship to the ornamental sweet peas.
description: Tuberous pea is a delicate climbing vine that uses curly tendrils to pull itself up through other plants, reaching about 4 feet tall. This perennial member of the legume family has a graceful, somewhat weak-stemmed appearance as it weaves through vegetation. It's quite rare in New England, with only a dozen recorded sightings, making it a special find for plant enthusiasts. The plant spreads underground through its characteristic tuber system, sometimes popping up in unexpected places.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Each leaf has exactly two oval leaflets and ends in a branched, twisting tendril that feels thin and wire-like to the touch - this tendril helps the plant climb

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to rose-colored pea-like flowers with the classic legume shape - a large upper petal (banner) and smaller side petals forming wings

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Weak climbing vine that leans on other plants for support, with thin green stems that feel soft and somewhat succulent when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Narrow, flattened pods typical of peas and beans, starting green and turning brown when ripe, containing several small round seeds

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Underground tubers along the root system that feel firm like small potatoes when dug up - a unique feature among New England climbing vines

habitat: Look for tuberous pea in disturbed soils, field edges, and areas with rich, moist earth in southern New England. It prefers spots where it can climb through other vegetation like fence rows, garden borders, or the edges of cultivated areas. This European native typically shows up in human-modified landscapes rather than deep wilderness.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground tubers, and the distinctive two-leaflet leaves with tendrils become visible as the plant begins its climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small pink pea flowers appearing, followed by the development of narrow seed pods. The plant reaches its full climbing height during this season.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and turn brown, while above-ground portions begin to die back. Underground tubers are actively storing energy for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: All above-ground parts have died back completely, but the tuberous root system remains alive underground, ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: The underground tubers of tuberous pea are actually edible and taste somewhat like chestnuts when cooked - in fact, they were cultivated as a food crop in parts of Europe and were sometimes called "Dutch mice" because people thought the tubers looked like little rodents!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other climbing Lathyrus species, but tuberous pea is the only one with exactly two leaflets per leaf AND underground tubers. Memory trick: "Two leaflets, tubers too!" Other sweet peas in the region either have more leaflets or lack the tuberous root system.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "pea," this plant is more closely related to sweet peas than garden peas. The "tuberous" part of its name refers to actual underground storage organs, not just thick roots - these tubers can persist for years and allow the plant to spread vegetatively even if the seeds don't germinate.
compareHints: Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system. The meadow pea has similar small leaflets but grows more upright and lacks tubers, while marsh pea prefers much wetter conditions and has more leaflets per leaf.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
